comments.text: Florida was never empty land waiting for concrete. Long before the first bulldozer, this peninsula was home to the Calusa, Tequesta, Ais, Apalachee, Timucua, and other Indigenous nations who had lived here for thousands of years. Later came the Seminoles — formed from Creek migrants, survivors of those earlier peoples, and runaway slaves seeking freedom. By the early 1800s, roughly 5,000 Seminoles lived across northern and central Florida.Then came the three Seminole Wars. The United States spent decades, tens of millions of dollars, and more than 1,500 soldiers’ lives trying to drive them out. Exact Native death tolls were never carefully recorded, but the result is clear: by 1858 the Seminole population in Florida had been reduced to a few hundred people, driven deep into the Everglades or shipped west. Starvation, disease, combat, and forced removal did the work. The land was cleared of its first inhabitants.That was the original “development.” What followed was a slower, more thorough version of the same logic. From Port St. Lucie south to Key West, we have taken wetlands, mangrove forests, and upland habitats and turned them into continuous concrete. The Indian River Lagoon, once one of the most biodiverse estuaries in North America, is now a stressed system of seagrass die-offs, algal blooms, and dead zones. The same pattern repeats down the coast: fill the marsh, dig the canal, pour the slab, sell the view.
